I also live with a lot of cats: they shed incessantly and create plenty of dust. I tried to manage for these things, but I need all the help I can get.That's where this pad has major pros.> It is very lightweight, which is perfect because I move the laptop a lot (petsitting....).> It is effective in helping my laptop manage overheating stress, but it's lost effectiveness over time (see cons below). It will only help to some degree; it will no longer allow my laptop to stop running its fan so hard as it once did.> The USB port functions even when the fans are switched off: I only have two USB ports and work with external HDs and an ergonomic mouse for wrist pain, so loosing a port would unreasonably inconveinance me. It does raise the level of the laptop surface, which can help with wrist angle in the right contexts, but it's not a change that significantly affects my ergonmic-y experiences. I need that wi-fi mouse.The major cons: some were immediate and some have developed as I've owned and used it.> The LED lights are pointless and wasteful, and most importantly for me, they're sleep disruptive. I'm a bit of an insomniac and one of my strategies to combat the difficulty in falling asleep is playing soothing audio through YouTube. If I can't sleep at all, I'll work on my laptop until I'm closer to the appropriate stage. Beacause of this, my laptop is stored right next to my bed, inside a high cabinet. Even through the cabinet door, the bright blue light spills  out into the room, and there's no way to turn it off and keep the fans on. On 80-90 degree nights, the fans have to be on to let my computer run safely and if the computer must be on so I can sleep, I'm screwed.> There is no way to fully clean the fans. Although the height and structure helps keep my laptop away from fuzz and dust, all that can go right into those pad fans. I can take off the mesh and do my best, but I can't access the center of the fans, where hairs would get wound up and caught.> That's responsible for some degree of the noise the fans began making after a year or so. At first it was intermittent and could be resolved by performing the minimal cleaning described above. The 'on' periods began getting longer until it never went away. For the last couple of years, it's settled into what I would call an aggressively loud tone: it always worries people, who think my laptop is about to explode. The noise certainly stifles any quiet, soothing audio I might want to play as a sleep aid, rather rendering the whole thing pointless for that capacity. I now use it predominantly as a flat, raised surface to keep my laptop off of cloth surfaces and only turn the fans on when I must to provide some help with those overheating symptoms in my laptop. So, it's better than a giant atlas...?>A negative side to the positive of its light construction is that the plastic is fairly fragile. The right side developed a crack next to the screw within months of normal use (I do want my things to last a long time and treat them with that in mind). The small plastic bars immediatly next to that crack were weakend and through normal use of gripping the sides to lift the laptop+pad, three of them have also broken.Overall, I'm disappointed in this pad: the long-term use isn't there because of its  design that doesn't allow basic maintenance and the fragility of the plastic itself. I hate the fact that I can't turn off those LED lights.I still have overheating issues with my laptop that need to be addressed, so despite owning one of these cooling pads, I'm still shopping for something more effective.

I chose this cooling pad due to the positive reviews on Amazon and YouTube, as well as the fact that the fan placement lines up well with the vents on the bottom of my MSI GF65. After testing it out, I can confirm that it makes a noticeable difference in the CPU temperature of my laptop (there wasn’t much point in running an idle test on the GPU.)First, I’ll give you the results of my CPU temp tests. Each condition below was tested three times (I did a grand total of 9 tests), so the numbers are the averages of the three tests conducted for that given condition. The details of my method are below the results:- Laptop flat on table: High 52.5 C (126.5 F), Low 47.5 C (117.5 F), Average 49.2 C (120.6 F)- Laptop On Havit Cooling Pad (pad fans OFF): High 50.3 (122.5 F), Low 44.3 C (111.7 F), Average 46.3 C (115.3 F)- Laptop on Havit Cooling Pad (pad fans ON): High 43.3 C (109.9 F), Low 37.7 C (99.86 F), Average 39.7 C (103.5 F)I ran some simple tests (surely not scientific, but I did my best) with my MSI GF65 at idle in order to compare three conditions: laptop flat on table, laptop on the Havit Cooling Pad (pad’s fans OFF), and laptop on the Havit Cooling Pad (pad’s fans ON.) In order to remove some potential variables, I turned off the computer’s Wifi, shut down all programs (except for Dragon Center to monitor temps,) moved the computer away from any AC draft or sunlight, and tested each condition three separate times. It’s also worth noting that the laptop was fully charged and running on the power adapter when these tests were performed. I did all three tests in a gauntlet fashion, such that round one was Table -> Pad Without Fans -> Pad With Fans…Round two was Table -> Pad Without Fans -> Pad With Fans etc. Each time I placed the laptop on a new surface, I let the computer sit for 10 minutes to allow its temperature to reach equilibrium. Then, I set a timer for 1 minute and recorded each temperature displayed during that minute. From these numbers I could get a high and low range as well as calculate the average temp. The results above are, themselves, the averages of the three tests of each condition.Besides the cooling effectiveness on my computer, the pad is quiet and very lightweight. I could see running this all the time without being fatigued by the gentle hum of the fans, and it’s portable enough to take just about anywhere in a laptop bag. Only complaint is that this design can’t be had with RGB! Does wanting cool lights make me a 10-year-old? Yes. Yes it does. (I have also tested Havit’s RGB model, which is a different design from the HV-F2056, and it performed significantly worse that this one. I’ll need to let function take precedence over form in this case.)

This is a typical, consumer-grade ethernet switch: they seem to work fine for a year or two, then they get buggy.  I tried the TP-Link 5 Port Gigabit Ethernet Network Switch for three reasons: (1) the metal housing hinted at above average construction; (2) they offered a useful warranty, in this case a "lifetime" limited warranty; and (3) I've had good luck with other TP-Link products, so I hoped this would would work too.Unfortunately, almost on schedule this switch started misbehaving about eighteen months after purchase.  It didn't actually fail dead, it just had to be "rebooted" a couple of times a day by unplugging the power for a few seconds.Usually this would have been right after the warranty expired.  But hey, I had this LIFETIME warranty, so I called their support number.  Well first, don't call them weekends or evenings because they keep strictly normal business hours.  Then when you do finally get through be very patient, because the service representatives speak very little English.  They will ask you to reconfigure the ethernet connections to the switch several ways, none of appear to make any sense.  Then if it does work (remember, I had an repeating, intermittent problem) they declare the problem solved, refuse to investigate further, and will not open a service ticket to track the problem.  So, when it recurred the next day (and the next after that, etc...) I would have togo through the whole thing again.  On one call I was actually told that the service representative had to leave: it was closing time and her shift was over, so I would have to call back the next day.After five tries I gave up on the warranty, and eventually gave up and replaced the switch.  TP-Link's switch is no better, and no worse, than several others I have used over the years.  Just don't believe their warranty: they know you really can't enforce it, and they have a system in place designed to wear you down so they don't have to honor it.

The TL-SG108E is a weird device. It's technically not a managed router but it offers a lot of the features of one. But in order to use these features you have to jump over an incredible number of technical hurdles. Especially if you don't run Windows. The retail box lies. Linux and Mac devices are not supported.TP-Link intentionally removed the web-interface for these so they don't compete with their managed router series. Instead you have to use their proprietary Java application that only works on one specific, ancient version of Java. And all the Java app does is connect to a non-standard webserver running on the device that it finds by UDP broadcast. But on any system other than Windows (which has a broken network stack in this regard) you have to set up ipv4 forwarding in your firewall and add specific rules so the crappy Java software can even find the switch.Once you've spent an hour and have all that set up you'll finally be able to change the default password to secure the switch. Configuration is done via the Java GUI but you can export as a configuration file. By manually editing this file you can make changes to the config but you still have to use the Java GUI to re-upload it.It's feature packed but those features are intentionally hamstringed by TP-Link to protect their more expensive managed switches. And unless you're technically adept you won't even be able to secure the device and use it as a normal switch. Actual performance is decent but the VLAN stuff, while obstensibly working, doesn't do network separation; an attacker on VLAN1 can spoof the ARP table for other VLANs. So it works but not for security, so it's useless.

It took some troubleshooting to figure out where to place it before it reached my devices successfully. The final location was NOT where the app initially suggested.Pros:-After an hour of troubleshooting, this finally did successfully get WiFi to the devices in the guest room. (Download 22.16Mb/s, Upload 0.31Mb/s, Ping 267ms, Jitter 11ms in the guest room with the extender.)-The physical installation is of course effortless. It simply plugs into the wall. No ethernet cable needed.-It is fairly small. Aesthetically adequate.Cons/Areas of Improvement:-The app should provide troubleshooting tips. After setup, an "I'm connected" button pops up, but I was not successfully connected at this point. I figured out how to improve the connection myself but there was no "I'm not connected" troubleshooting button.-The app persistently told me that the device was perfectly located even though my devices showed that there was no Internet connected.-The device will continue to show all green LEDs even when no devices are detecting an Internet connection. This continued even when the device was right next to the extender.-In trying to connect my smart TV, it kept telling me the wireless strength was "Good" but failed to work because there was no Internet connection. This was while my laptop was connected to the same network, so I knew the Internet connection was intact in the same room.-The extension WiFi frequently stops working on my phone. It either disappears altogether or says "Internet not available."-To set up "High Speed Mode," the "Auto (Recommended)" option does NOT work. The only way I was finally able to get WiFi to my devices in the guestroom was to use "Manual," then Router-to-Extender in 2.4GHz only and Extender-to-Client in 5GHz only. It was only after I made this change and moved the extender closer to the guest room that all my devices registered that the Internet was connected.OVERALL:This can serve the purpose of eliminating a dead zone so is worth buying in my opinion. I just bought two of these to change one ethernet cable into two.  Huh?  Simple  - I have an ethernet cable connecting two parts of my house.  Want it to behave like two cables- one on the Internet, the other one on my private net.The reasonable and ordinary way to accomplish this is to use VLANs.  You set up a VLAN that is port-based, and also tagged.  So ports 1 and 2 might be on VLAN 2, and ports 3 & 4 on VLAN 3.  VLANs 2 and 3 then squirt (now tagged) out another port which goes to the other end of the cable - where another switch converts them into port-based again.So you wind up with a system that looks like two Ethernet cables, when you really only have one.  This saves you from having to run the second cable.It's a fairly common and ordinary use case.UNFORTUNATELY,  although this unit supports both port-based and tagged VLANS, it will not do both at the same time.  You can have port-based....OR you can have tagged.  But not both.  Makes it useless for my purpose.

Overall, I'm very impressed with this switch's features and wrestled with the three star rating.  You really shouldn't expect more at this price point and so far, it works as advertised.  Unfortunately there is a pretty big security flaw in the web interface that could be leveraged to defeat your network segmentation.  Hoping to see a firmware fix, but until then, just be aware of it and understand the risk.Specifically, the switch IP that hosts the http tcp/80 web interface can not be turn off or restricted to any specific ports or vlans.  That IP exists on all ports and vlans regardless of how you segment everything else.  This opens up an attack vector that could easily defeat you network segmentation.  Since mac addresses are vendor specific, an attacker can just sweep RFC-1918 address space to discover TP link devices then spoof scan for port 80 to discover targets.  It wouldn't take too long to brute force the authentication and add themselves to the money vlan.  It took me about an hour to run a POC with off the shelf network tools.  I'm guessing this is something a motivated attacker would have in their toolbelt.That said, it would probably take a motivated attacker or someone skilled and bored with access to a public network.EDIT:  The best protection you could add right away would be to use a randomized 16 char password and username.  Unfortunately they only allow letters, numbers, digits and underscore up to 16 chars in each field, but randomizing both should at least make the brute force attack more difficult.

This switch works and is not too expensive, but for something billed as a managed switch, it sure seems to be missing some basic functionality.First off, I would expect a managed switch to have full support for Ethernet's spanning tree protocol (STP).  However, this switch lacks the ability to set the switch priority, which means if you want to use this as your root switch, you have to go increase the priority of every other switch in your network.  And if you have a second switch that won't let you set priority, well then you'll just get something random based on the switch MAC addresses.  You can designate a root port, but that's not what I need in my root switch.Second, there doesn't seem to be any ability to configure trunking on ports when you are using 802.1Q VLAN tags.  If you happen to use a small number of VLANs, you can go through the laborious process of manually configuring a port to be a "tagged" member of each individual VLAN.  But I don't really want to do that 4000 times (and something tells me the software would limit me well below 4096 VLANs).One disclaimer is that I use linux, not Windows, so I'm using the web interface, not the configuration software.  Nonetheless, a search of the PDF configuration utility manual finds zero occurences of the word "trunk."  Another disclaimer is that every other managed switch I've bought has had a lot more ports, so it's conceivable that every other 8-port switch on the market is similarly limited.  One of the reasons I bought this switch is that it's part of a product line that goes up to 48 ports, so I figured the software should support features I expect from larger switches.  Sadly, that logic definitely work out.So read the manual before buying something, and take the description of "Abundant VLAN features" with a grain of salt, because they aren't so abundant as to include trunking...

I bought this switch to use specifically with an amateur radio Broadband Hamnet mesh network, as I needed tagging for a few select ports.  The switch showed up in fine fashion and is well built; however, upon further investigation, I discovered that when operating the switch using 802.1p, VLAN 1 is a default configuration that can't be changed.  Many other routers have standard names for VLAN 1 that can't be changed, but the firmware in this switch doesn't allow ANY changes to any settings or ports under VLAN 1, making this switch unusable for BBHN applications as of the current BBHN firmware (v3.1.0).  If BBHN changes their firmware in future releases to allow users to custom select VLAN numbers for WAN, Node-2-Node, and User traffic, then this switch will work fine for that, but as of now, it's unsuitable for BBHN/AREDN mesh network applications.

I got this to use in AP (Access Point) mode, meaning with a wired connection to the main router. If your building allows this, it will give much better performance than Extender mode. I actually set it up in Extender mode with Tether, and then switched it to AP mode in Tether (it could be easier to find this option in the app) and plugged in the wired network after. Then I found out that the auto channel selector in the 5 GHz band selects the worst channel instead of the best, and Tether seems to lack a way to override it. So I had to use the Web (http) interface to manually select a 5 GHz channel that did not conflict with the main router. But the RE220 has solved the main problem I had, which was that the older / cheaper TP-Link Extender I had been using kept refusing connections, probably because it secretly had an 8 connection hard limit. Its a switch! Does what it needs to do.Pros:* Runs cold to the touch even when under decent load with multiple devices so its probably very energy efficient.* Seems to be very high performance! No latency or bandwidth changes vs direct CAT6a connection on gigabit ethernet. Tested with up to 3 devices under load. Latency was statistically unchanged and bandwidth/QoS was what you'd expect on paper so overhead is super low and on board protocols are implemented extremely well! Grain of salt though...  I haven't formally benchmarked or even really used SOHO switches since the 10/100 days. Maybe all makes/models are similar nowadays, but 20 years ago using switches was only a tad  better than a hub in terms collision prevention and simple QoS.* Physical build quality is top notch, with one caveat (see Cons)Cons:* Design of metal casing is probably perfect for mounting on the side of standard 1U or 2U racks, warehouse racks, or anything else with standardized screw hole placement and (ideally) the ability to come in from behind or at least see what you're doing. I needed to mount this to a wall in my home office where I couldn't just screw into a rack with standard mounts and slide the switch in place 5 seconds later.There may be a much better way, but the only solution I could come up with (in order to use the rubber feet as standoffs to allow airflow) was to take the housing apart and unscrew/remove the PCB to see what the correct distance between screws needed to be. In theory this would be the last step but unfortunately problem #2 (really the only roadblock in retrospect) was that when wall mounting, the shape of the mounting cutouts are such that you (or at least me?)don't give you enough "turning radius" to get the switch mounted without the offset from the screw head and the wall surface being stupidly long.The only solution where the standoff distance was both far enough to get the screw heads in there while ALSO getting it to mount securely without flapping around loose was to clip the opening a bit with sheet metal snips. This was a tad challenging but doable, mostly because of the cramped areas for maneuver.My recommended wall mount steps (unless someone has a better way) are:1. Insert the screws in the mounting holes, and position in the narrower "top" area where they loosely stay in place when held in by hand. This will be the distance when mounted.  2. Gently press the switch and screws into the wall just enough to create 2 small dents so you know where to drill.3. Drill. I didn't need a drywall screw due to wood paneling, but use drywall screws if bare drywall. If you think you don't need to just do it anyway. Its cheap, easy, and a good best practice to prevent yanks from plugged in devices, etc.4. Screw the screws in 95% of the way. You may be able to just mount the switch ok. If not, you may need to do step 5...5. (Optional). If necessary AND you know what you're doing, AND you don't care about warranties, open up the mounting cavity with metal snips, but only after you have unscrewed the device housing and have carefully removed all the (guts). Put them aside in an anti static bag to keep them safe.Start by clipping tiny slivers from the two mounting cavities on the bottom device housing piece. Adjust the screw depth until you can easily mount the housing without it feeling loose. You may need to test/adjust a few times, since the screw head will be blocked by sheet metal. This is the core design flaw, otherwise you could just (at worst) unscrew the top housing cover, remove the "guts", and just screw it in by hand, with the final step being to put everything back together (annoying but simple if you own magnetic screwdrivers).Again, only do this if no viable alternatives exist for you, as I'm sure it voids the warranty.Conclusion? Buy this excellent product, just be prepared for a "project" if this is going on a wall in a SOHO setting.

I was excited about this camera and it worked as advertised for about a week. Then one morning I came into my office and it didn't alert upon me entering. I couldn't get it to trigger with motion no matter what I did. This continued more days than not. If I opened the app and did a live view, it would "wake up" and work, but any time the IR turned on in the dark, it would subsequently not turn off as it should, so once there was light again, the screen could not sense motion because the IR was stuck on (IR + light = white screen).Upon contacting support (after many other unrelated troubleshooting steps), they informed me "the issue you are experiencing is the known issue about blink mini where it doesn't detect motion and displays red" and "we are still working to get this fixed because the way this camera is designed is the reason why this known issue is created. Basically, this happens when there are rapid light changes in front of the camera, especially in the garage, when you open the door or turn on the light, these can cause the IR filter to get stuck, and the motion won't work unless you issue a command."I can say from my experience that the issue is not limited to rapid light changes. I have a window in my office, and every night when it gets dark, the IR comes on. Then, when the sun rises, the IR refuses to turn off and the camera gets stuck. I can "issue a command" (basically interact with the camera in any way through the app) to get the camera to work again, but I wanted reliable notifications of motion without having to remember to open the app every day and do a live view some time after sunrise.Support did offer that I could do a scheduled disarm/arm command so this interaction would happen automatically, but scheduling it to arm when it was already armed didn't work, and disarming then arming it would require 15 minutes of downtime between the two commands. While the likelihood of anything being missed during those 15 minutes was very low, I purchased a camera based on the promise of uninterrupted monitoring, which this does not provide. I also have no good way of knowing when to schedule a command like that since I don't know at what point it becomes "stuck" as the sun comes up, and that time would change throughout the year and based on weather. Amazon kindly returned it for me outside of the return window (since the return window closed before we got to the "known issue" in troubleshooting).If you don't need IR or automatic motion detection after the IR has been triggered and before you interact with the camera, this would probably be a good camera for you. I essentially wanted a security camera in an office during the day and night, and while this was advertised as that, it isn't until they fix this issue.

While the camera will transition from day to night, the Blink mini (firmware 9.70) will not transition from night to day. Even with sufficient light on in the room with sunrise, the IR sensor remains on and motion is not detected so recording does not happen. Even at night if a light is turned on in the room, the camera will not transition from IR sensing to daylight mode and so will not detect motion. A security camera foiled by turning on a light! Evidently this is a long running issue with this mini camera as it was reported over a year ago now.It seems not fit for purpose.The only ways to work around this seem to be:1. Manually trigger a photo, live view, or disarm and immediately re-arm. This takes manual intervention and must be timed with sufficient day light in the space.2. Set a schedule to disarm and then rearm the camera. This results in at least 15 minutes of potentially lost recordings since schedules can only be set at 15 minute increments. (Maybe an Alexa routine can do this automatically with less of a gap in recording?)3. Turn off night vision mode and rely on a secondary light. So keep the camera in normal daylight mode at all times. Some use a separate motion detection light to turn on so that recording at night can still work.None of these seem like good enough solutions.Called support today and they said they were aware and working on the issue, but had no estimate on when it would be resolved. Maybe after a year of this being a known issue they can't resolve it at all?

I have (or have had) Arlo, Blink, EZViz and Wyze cameras, and I have settled on Wyze for my indoor and outdoor system. The Blink Mini is a decent camera, but the unacceptable flaw for me is the inability to watch SD card video (from the Sync Module2) through the app. Incredibly, it seems you have to remove the SD card from the sync module to view video stored on it from a device. Each of my Wyze v3 Cams has its own SD card, and I am able to see alert footage stored in the Wyze cloud and/or extended continuous footage from each camera's SD card through the Wyze app. If I see a Wyze alert video clip that ends before I want it to, or if I need to see events immediately preceding the alert clip, I can switch to PLAYBACK view and watch what is recorded continuously on the SD card for whatever length of time I want through the app. Also, the Blink Minis randomly stop recording events, and require power cycling before they will restart. The Arlo cameras had this same issue, and I junked them as a result. If you're away from home, as on vacation, and one of the cameras stops recording, you're out of luck until someone can power cycle the individual camera that has stopped recording motion. Not acceptable. The 7 Wyze v3 Cams have been extremely stable over a period of five months. The Wyze v3 Cams are priced about the same as the Blink Minis at this writing. I see no reason to accept the deficiencies of the Blink Minis when the Wyze V3 Cams are so much better. So I am replacing my 3 Blinks with additional Wyze v3s.

Then I download the application and try to connect the camera to my mobile devices.  It takes 2-4 tries before it connects, then it asks for a password.  Again, NOTHING in the directions about this.  Back to You Tube for another 45 minutes until I find a video that  provides the password as 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,0.  So 2+ hours to do what should have taken 15 minutes.Now to the operation.  I had a tough time turning the camera on in the case.  It would take pressing the button hard 4+ times before it would turn on and in some cases, I had to take it out of the case to turn it on. I would think these companies could hire someone to do a 5-minute You Tube tutorial, but I suspect these cameras are sold under 50 names and all have variables that would make any consistent directions impossible to provide.  After this experience, I purchased a GoPro and had it set up in 15 minutes.  If you have the time to research all the Bermuda Triangle stuff associated with these off brand action cameras, then purchase and save the money.  If your time and sanity are worth more than $100 in savings, then purchase a GoPro.

The video and audio quality far exceeded my expectations! The motion detection is good,  but not consistent. The night-vision is better than expected.  The zoom feature is the same as taking a picture on your phone & zooming in.  You are limited to the extent of the picture and it becomes grainy. The audio is very clear and decent range. The two outdoor cameras can also be saved to a separately purchased usb drive that plugs into the module.  Beyond those options,  I have no way to view or save my videos from my indoor/outdoor cameras.  I am also disappointed that the app only let's you view live view for 30 seconds at  a time & not a continuous stream.  Also disappointing is that the app only let's you view streams one at a time,  rather than having a multi-panel view.  Unfortunately,  these issues are big shortcomings  in what I feel are important and fundamental functions & purpose of any camera system.Although these issues are big disappointments to me,  I am still happy with the overall capabilities and functions of these cameras at this price point. I bought this camera for someone who is not a techie and had no prior vlogging or making action videos.  I did have to help them use the QR code included with the device and download the PDF manual for them.  But afterward, this person was able to quickly get setup within 30 mins, on their own.They said they really liked the simple and lightweight nature of the design and even could simply strap it to the their wrist while walking.  The menu is relatively intuitive, using a combination of the 4 buttons (front, top, up, & down), but for more granular settings, have to figure things out through some simple trial and error.The screen on the back of the camera is bright enough for indoor use and covers the entire back of the camera, but is difficult to see if outside in the sun.  But the good news is it's NOT a touchscreen.  This is actually a good thing because the camera is so so small, that pressing buttons or going the menus is difficult without accidentally touching that back screen.The video output is only (.mov) file format, but this is not an issue for simple playback on almost any computer.The battery was ok on a full-charge (about 2+ hours), but if you use the rear screen to change settings a lot, it seems to drain the battery much faster.  Leaving the power plugged-in for a long-time does make the camera very hot, and I wouldn't recommend it.  The person I bought this for, tried it in their car using a usb charger, and used it that way, but said they would not recommend continuously recording for more than a couple of hours.Pros:--Whole thing is very light and has a rubberized exterior.  Dropped it a few times onto hard floors and no issues.--Verified 1080p quality video looks good even when projected onto wide screens.--Does have good stabilization, having seen videos of both walking and driving in a car on rural roads.--Does take good cell-phone quality standard photos also.--Includes accessories like external charging dock and two batteries, at this price.--Tested and works with microSD cards at 32gb, 64gb, or128gb (all were Class 10, U3).--Simply file/folder setup after formatting the memory card.  Two folders found on the microSD - Videos & Photos.  Was easily able to transfer to a Mac or a PC.--Has two small micro-USB ports on the side of the camera.  Can use one for transferring files from camera, and the other for plug-in power.Cons:--Microphone is not good at all, even at close distances, like 5 feet away, and also picks up a lot of wind noise.--Microphone audio is muffled when enclosed in the included clear case.  Had to leave the camera un-cased in order to get proper audio.--Also, there's no option for plugging-in an external mic.--Does not come with an included manual.  Have to go to a site and download the PDF.--Not good for night shooting, including indoors that have low-light areas.This is really a camera to buy for beginners who are just learning about vlogging or want something simple for action shots, or even as a backup or second camera.

I bought this for my nephew who is 12. I have a gopro hero 7 black and he loves using my gopro he is just rougher than i like on the camera after watching his footage. I formatted the card in the camera and that is when this started, I put the card in un-formatted the night it arrived it recorded without any issues. Here is what I found I bought him a class 10 U3 64gb Samsung card with 100mb/s write speed the card is good for 4k I checked it against fakes it's a legit Samsung sd card. If you press record and your Akaso Ek7000 freezes or throws lines across the screen back down the resolution what we found worked was 1080p 30 frames anything higher and the camera freaked out. To format the card or change reolution once powered on press the mode button until the wrench is displayed then press the top record button. Once inside settings the mode button exits and the record button is enter the side buttons scroll. with Resolution highlighted press the record button set it to 1080/30 then press mode button to exit out of settings. The app I can't get to work on an iPhone 8+ or a Samsung S8+ i only connected successfully once it froze.I could return the camera but recording in 1080/30 will be fine for a 12yo it takes photos just fine this is a test to see if he will take care of it then I will get him an official GoPro. My nephews love the springs and they film fish, turtles and back flips off the dock with my gopro but now they have their own to use and my GoPro is no longer bounced off the bottom or banging against the rails climbing up the dock. Hopefully this helps someone i couldn't find anything on a freezing or lines across the screen for the Akaso brand.

I bought this card to use for 4K video recordings with my new Nikon Z 5. Since I don't always see this or am there when it happens this is a serious problem.This is speculation on my part but I believe this error happens when the camera cannot write to the card fast enough.  The internal buffers overflow on the camera and it is forced to stop recording or deliver a broken poor quality choppy video.  It chooses the former hence the error.  I purchased this card specifically because it advertises itself as being fast enough to record 4K video.  Yet my much older Sandisk Ultra with lower advertised specs has no problem meeting these needs.  I verified through some well known tools that the card I received was genuine so this seems to be a defect in the design of the card itself.  After writing to the card in its entirety it is expected to become slower and I suspect that's why the issue didn't appear early on.

I just wanted a cheap way to ensure if someone lurks around/breaks in, I have a chance at catching an image of who they are.A few things to think about:1. You must have working Wi-Fi with an Internet connection.  This sounds stupid, but my modem went out the other day, so I still had a working Wi-Fi network, but that is not good enough.  While my Hue lights still worked without working Internet, my Blink cameras did not.If you want hard core security cameras, these aren't going to be your best option. Someone could very easily kill your cameras without even having to go inside your house/business.2. While I haven't tried it yet, I believe your recordings go to the Blink servers even when you don't have a subscription.  They mention you can backup the clips set off by movement, but given it "backs those clips up once daily by default" to the thumb drive attached to the Sync Module 2, it must be temporarily storing those clips on their server (which is why you would need the Internet - See point 1 above).  So if it bothers you that Amazon will still have access to those clips, you may want to investigate other options.3.  Think about how where to install the cameras.  It actually does better when someone/something moves across the field of vision as per their instructions.  They are correct.  What I mean by this is imagine you are looking at a device screen.  It works best if the image moves across the screen from left to right or right to left.  Coming straight at the camera doesn't set it off as quickly as I would expect.  While the camera I have can see the sidewalk out by the street, I was practically at the door before it started recording.  So you have to think about how to get the motion detection to get the camera to start recording while at the same time having a good angle to get a good picture of a person's face.  -- I haven't tried to see if there are some sensitivity options to try to get the camera to go off sooner.4. They need to provide a longer cord.  I was going to install it to the ceiling to get the "right" angle to cover two doors close to one another.  Even if I went straight from the outlet to the ceiling, the cord isn't long enough to then mount to the ceiling.  Trying to get it to move into the corner was impossible.Again, I am going for low cost security.  I really just wanted to make sure no one is coming up to the door when we aren't around.  If I had great security concerns, I would keep exploring other options.

I have several of both the Minis and the outdoor models, and this Mini is almost identical to the outdoor and indoor models in terms of quality and features. The only real difference between them is the Mini isn't weather-proof, cannot handle the extreme temperatures of the outdoor models (-4 to 113 F), has a better mount, can be image-flipped, and runs solely on a power adapter instead of batteries.* Not Weather-proof: DO NOT use this mini camera outdoors or in an uninsulated building. It is not water-proof and will likely be damaged by humidity and high or low temperatures.* Mount & Image Flipping: this mount is great and allows easier installation locations than the indoor and outdoor cameras, because it's mounted from the bottom/top instead of the back.  Since this Mini can be mounted from the bottom or top, this means it can be turned at many more angles on all 3 axes than the Indoor/Outdoor. If you have to mount it upside-down, such as from a ceiling, the app simply allows you to flip the image vertically. The problem with the indoor/outdoor models is the mounting is on the back, which means you can't "hang" it from a ceiling and point it in any direction. Instead, if you want to mount the Indoor/Outdoor on a ceiling or near the ceiling, you have a very small angle to point it. This makes the Indoor/Outdoor cameras inconvenient to install from above in most situations because you'll end up having to point the camera directly outward from your mounting surface. If from a ceiling, it'll face down. If from the top of a wall, it'll face outward along the ceiling. The Mini's mount is much better.CONS:* The "Talk" feature is totally useless. Regardless of bandwidth or proximity to the router or a sync module (purchased separately), the Talk feature produces broken sound that is impossible to understand. Plus there's a long delay of 3-6 seconds, making this feature useless for conversations, even if the other person understood anything you were saying. Over several tests with all of our different Blink cameras, none of them produce clear enough speech that someone can understand you, no matter where the cameras are located.* No wired Ethernet option. This camera can only be used with a wireless router and Internet connection. There are no other options.* Cannot be used as a USB web cam* Cannot be used for continuous live feeds. The live feed only allows up to 30 seconds of viewing, and you must hit a Continue button every 30 seconds to keep it going. So if need a camera to leave running for frequent live video, Blink isn't what you're looking for.* Cloud Storage Subscription semi-requirement: the Blink Home Monitor App's features become limited if you don't purchase a cloud storage subscription. If you stick with the Sync Module for local storage and do not purchase any of the cloud storage plans, VIDEO CLIPS CANNOT BE VIEWED THROUGH THE APP. The app will only allow you to view the live feed, adjust camera settings, and use the Talk feature. Without a cloud storage subscription, the only way to view your camera's video clips is by physically taking your USB storage device (purchased separately) out of the Sync Module (purchased separately) and placed in a USB port on a computer (purchased separately).To be very clear here, if you do not purchase a cloud storage subscription, you will not be able to view any of the stored video clips (including motion-activated clips) from your phone. Period. This point has not been made clearly anywhere in the advertisements, support screens, Amazon product pages, or Blink Web site, but it's a crucial piece of information that the company is being very ambiguous about.To repeat, IF YOU DON'T PURCHASE A CLOUD STORAGE SUBSCRIPTION, YOU CANNOT VIEW YOUR VIDEO CLIPS THROUGH YOUR PHONE. I have seen some reviewers assert that this isn't technically possible, but as a software engineer I know this isn't true. The Blink developers clearly focused on developing the cloud storage and subscriptions, using the mobile app as the user's "portal" app to access and view the cloud-stored video clips, and have simply decided not to develop a mechanism for the mobile app to access the video clips stored in your Sync Module. I want to be very clear here....this IS POSSIBLE and would require a lot of development to accomplish, but Blink just doesn't provide this functionality (yet). Whether they are working on this feature and plan to add it in the future is unknown. But the lack of direct integration between the mobile app and the Sync Module's local storage (over the local network, especially) is a significant shortcoming in the entire Blink system. This also means that if your camera loses its internet connection, it will not capture video, you can't view the live feed, the Talk feature won't work, and you can't change the camera's settings.. The Blink system simply does not allow the mobile app to connect directly to a camera or Sync Module on your local network. It is designed to use the Internet only. This is a very important point that customers must understand. Both the camera and the Sync Module require an active Internet connection to function. They will not work independently or with just a wifi router. Internet is required.

A couple thoughts on this item. I received it a day early than expected so the shipping was great. It didn't come in an original iPhone box however it wasn't damaged in any way. The condition was perfect. I was pretty happy with it. Put in a Verizon sim and it picked up the Verizon network pretty much immediately. Then put it on charge to charge up and updated the operating system.This is when things went south. The battery ran super hot when charging. A lot more hot than normal. I then tried typing in the phone's IMEI number into Verizon's website and was told that the phone is not compatible with Verizon. I did this more than once just to make doubly sure I had typed it in correctly.I then tried to make a call. The call quality was terrible. At times it was impossible to hear anything. It didn't matter if the call was on speaker or not. I tried restarting the phone and got pretty much the same result. When trying to make a call, it spoke a lot about roaming. This was key. I turned the roaming option off and tried again. Still talking about roaming.This phone was not 100% unlocked. It was probably locked to a network such as AT&T or T-Mobile at some stage, however it lacks the antenna which will allow it to connect to other networks such as Verizon or Sprint. A phone which is 100% unlocked will have antenna built into it which support all the networks making it a fully unlocked phone. The phone did pick up Verizon, however that was based on roaming on some other network and not by connecting directly to any Verizon tower in my area.A fully unlocked phone would have shown on Verizon's website that the IMEI number was compatible with their network. It would have also come back as being compatible with AT&T's network as well as T-Mobile and Sprint. It would have saved me time and money if the IMEI number was checked by the seller as to whether it was compatible with the Verizon network instead of running an unlock code on the phone and then marketing it as being fully unlocked.I checked the IMEI number. It came back clean however it does show that it comes from a phone which has 128 GB of storage. This phone has 32 GB of storage, so somewhere there is a discrepancy. I suspect the phone may have been made up from parts from various phones.I sent the phone back.

I've bought two of these, but not for a good reason... the first one I got from a seller named BuySPRY and unfortunately it looks like they don't repair the phones they work on correctly. I didn't really take concern about this until after I spilled a glass of water on my table, some of which went onto the phone. These phones are rated IP67 water resistant, but this particular phone repaired by BuySPRY was not properly sealed.If you do a little research you find these phones require you to remove all the old adhesive between the phone screen and the phone chassis and install a fresh new one; this is one of the primary things maintaining water resistance among a few other details. Anyway this phone clearly had not had its screen adhesive replaced, there was chunks of it exposed going around the edges of the screen - which left just enough of a gap for water to ingress.The big sad thing here is this happened I'm not kidding one day after the 90 warranty ended. I contacted the seller to inform them of the problem and asked if they could do anything. They didn't at all seem concerned their phone wasn't repaired correctly, nor did they offer any form of compensation for their poorly repaired device.So I ended up buying a new one, from a different seller named Hybrid IT. It has been over a month now and I so far have had a good experience. The first phone I got had a poor health battery as indicated in iPhone battery information. I contacted the seller about it; and they immediately corrected the problem. They sent me another phone which has a 100% battery. So far this phone has been perfect and I haven't had any issues with it. I also can clearly see the screen adhesive looks like it is brand new. Hopefully this one will hold out.Moral to the story, if you at all find anything concerning with your purchase of an Amazon renewed phone... don't hesitate, don't take chances... get them to make it right. Some of us are more picky than others, but my main concerns on repaired phones are the water tight seal and the health of the battery. It is going to be very difficult to find a perfect condition used phone, so you have to pick what you care about most. Good luck!

BATTERY LIFE YO. I bought this specifically for the long lasting battery. After an ice storm last winter and being out of power for a week I realized how trash my old phones battery was, it wouldn't even last a day. I know that sounds like a bit much, but I'm a budget buyer, not a power user, and for the money spent, this was more than worth the price.  It's battery life has been excellent, as expected, even with heavy out-bound media streaming and long, long drives with navigation enabled.  On an average work day from a full charge I barely use 20% of the battery before it gets recharged at night.  I have only seen the battery get below 50% once, during one of those long drives I mentioned.  Nearly a year on, and the battery capacity is still very, very good.This is an "Anywhere" phone that is unlocked for all service providers on both major network systems, though finding the right sim card was a little involved.  It had a fairly unmodified Android 10 installation when purchased, and did get an OTA update to Android 11 since purchased.  I have also gotten regular updates to the OS as they become available.  Motorola has been very good about pushing out security updates when needed.  Wifi and Bluetooth operation have been consistently very good.  4G LTE operation is very strong.  Something I would expect from the company that almost founded mobile communications.As a budget phone it is NOT the fastest, nor most beautiful phone you can buy.  It's outer case is plastic, but the screen is reasonably bright and crisp, and the sound is better than most with actual stereo speakers.  The audio hardware on board is better than average with a quality DAC that music apps like Power Amp can truly utilize to good advantage.  It has three rear facing cameras, including Macro, and wide-angle lenses.  Even the selfie cam is pretty good.  The flash is nice and bright and even doubles as a flashlight with just a shake.  It has a decent amount of Ram, and on-board storage, with a Micro SD card slot for more.  I expect that I will be carrying this phone for a couple more years before Google's app updates eat all of it's storage.The only downsides to this phone, for me, are not uncommon for most phones these days:  The battery is not user replaceable, and there is no physical keyboard.  Two features I -really- miss from my older phones.

Best hope your phone's got internet, otherwise you can't access ANY of that data outside the summary screen. The perfect adventure watch for those of us who never leave 4G coverage, I guess?Did I say app? I meant appS. App zoo. App swarm. Oooh no, wait, got it: APP-ocalypse.If you want to track calories, you will need to download a separate app. If you want to connect that data to a smart scale (unless you buy the Garmin smart scale [that requires a WIFI connection to function?!] for $100+), you'll need another app (besides the one that comes to the scale) to connect that. And if you want to fully utilize the watch's (limited and confusing) GPS features, you'll need another app for that. Most of them require separate accounts, all of them refuse to function unless you give them access to basically all the data on your phone.Basically, if you've ever thought the Fitbit app was nice, but it would be better split into 5 apps from 4 developers, with really, really, predatory app permissions (especially MyFitnessPal -- can't track your calories unless you enable microphone permissions, yeah ok, seems legit) this is the watch for you.Summary: If you're thinking about buying this watch as a fitness tracker, don't. You'll need an entire app suite to get basic functionality and after all that you'll just be looking at wildly inaccurate data. If you're thinking about buying this watch to use as a GPS device, don't. You'll get lost and die. The only thing this watch does reliably is tell you the time and date, which any $20 Timex does just as well.

I stop and count my rate and find it over 100.  Also, it rarely reports the high number to the ap correctly.  I will be hiking and see a high of 150 and at the end when I review the data on the app the says my high was 138.  The elevation gain always reads way higher than it is.  I have another app on my phone (All Trails) that I compare to the watch and the phone will tell me I gained 2000 feet and the watch will say 3800 feet (not possible).  There are times when the watch time gets stuck at moment; I will look at the time and it says 9:32 and I realize that is not possible I look at my phone and sure enough its actually 10:30.  Once I push a couple of buttons on the watch it corrects itself. Battery life – forget what the reviews say or what Garmin promotes as long battery.  The life is all based on how long and how many activities you track in a given period.  The only way you can get 14 days is if you have no activities.  The battery last about 6 to 8 hours of activity.  There is a meter on the watch that shows you bars but don’t trust the bars it can show 3 bars and within a couple of hours I am running out of power.  What they should do is tell you how much time remains based on activities (they could do this in the app).  After 5 months I have started having the watch regularly stop tracking my heart rate in the app and in the watch.  It will report a number but the graph is gone and it does not report it to the phone.  I must reboot it two or three times to get it to work.  I have tried the cleaning instructions, but it hasn't helped at all.  If you are looking for a watch that is cool looking then this is it otherwise forget this watch.

I compared it with other watches, my phone, and known distance courses, several times running with one on each wrist, and comparing distance with my husband who would run with me.  Without fail, the Instinct was shorter, often several 10th's of a mile per mile, which really adds up when you're looking at running/hiking 10, 20, 30+ miles.  The bottom line is this watch is unusable as a training aid.I contacted Garmin shortly after purchasing the watch looking into replacement options.  All I wanted was to send it back and get credit towards a different Garmin watch.  Because I bought the watch through a third party, Garmin was unwilling to help me in anyway.  The third party proved very difficult to work with, offering to exchange it but then making the process nearly impossible and basically ignoring my questions until I finally gave up. Now, I am stuck with a barely used, two-hundred forty dollar paperweight.As a Garmin fan, I am extremely disappointed in the customer service I received from Garmin, and the quality of the Garmin Instinct.  The watch itself is rugged, well-built, and attractive but accuracy is the #1 most important feature of a GPS watch and this one falls flat on its face.

I cannot understand why the major manufacturers of this type of equipment can’t give us a simple privacy control option to just keep our data. I have been using Garmin GPS products for years for boating, biking, running and hiking.  I recently bought a Garmin Instinct to replace a Fore Runner 230 that I have been using for running and general fitness tracking for about 3 years.  I really liked the FR230 but wanted to get some additional features such as heart rate and built in navigation.The Instinct has worked well as a replacement in most of its features but I did start to notice that the distance I was running was shorter than before.  It also seemed like my minutes per mile were much slower.  Initially I chalked this up to the heart rate feature because I was trying to run to the heart rate.  However, after taking a moment to compare the Instinct miles for my normal running coarse to a previous run with my FR230 I noticed the Instinct was substantially less than the FR230.So I wore both the Instinct and the FR230 and went for a run on my normal coarse.  Sure enough, the FR230 showed 4.42 miles ran and the Instinct was 4.11 miles.  This is a substantial difference and I wasn't 100% sure which watch to believe.  So I wore both watches and drove the same coarse in the car measuring distance with the digital odometer.  When I did that both watches were at 4.4 and 4.42 miles which agreed with the car.So it appears as though the Instinct didn't measure my distance accurately while running but did while driving the same coarse.I reached out to Garmin support and was told to delete the running app from the list of apps and then add it back in.  (I was already at the most recent software update.)  I was shocked that this was suggested as I figured it would not do anything and specifically said so.  However, I was assured this would fix it and I was also told there were no bad batches or problems that may have affected my watch.This did not fix it and I am disappointed that my time was even wasted doing something so minor to try to fix a problem like this.  Needless to say, regardless of how good the watch may be in other features, being off by around 10% in its accuracy for running is a show stopper.  So I rate this watch a 1 and would suggest steering away from it if you plan to use it for anything like running or hiking or basically much of what it was designed to do.I have also looked at some of the forums and have seen posts from others who are having similar problems.

This resulted in it calculating a distance travelled which was almost double what it should have been.I contacted Garmin technical support, and they advised that I shouldn't use UltraTrac in "severe conditions" which included "trees, mountains or water". I would assume that most people who require the additional battery life would be passing through areas like this, so this wasn't particularly helpful.Another more minor but still annoying issue was when using the watch with a planned course. Whenever I deviated from the track by even a small distance (or the watch thought I had) then the watch would buzz to notify I was off-course, and then again to say I was on-course. This happened constantly, even when I wasn't actually moving, just from GPS inaccuracies. It is possible to turn off the "off-course" notifications, but bizarrely I would still get the "on-course" notification. Only way to avoid was to turn on do not disturb mode on the watch, and lose all the other notifications too. It wasn't possible to adjust the sensitivity.I also contacted technical support about this issue. All they would do was put in a "feature" request, which may or may not ever get implemented. Considering that this seems to have been a known issue for years based on forum threads I found, I wouldn't be hopeful, and I will probably avoid Garmin for my replacement watch.

Let's start with the good parts. This watch packs a huge amount of capabilities in a tiny package that's rugged and comfortable to wear all day. And it's not too expensive.The watch has dozens of screens packed with useful information for fitness and outdoor activities. Weather, sunrise/sunset, compass, altimeter, step counter, calorie counter, heart rate graphs, and on and on. Plus customized screens for a dozen or so different sports: running, trail running, road biking, mountain biking, climbing, strength training, etc.Every one of these screens can be configured to show exactly the data you want. And that's the first problem. Unless you just want to use the defaults, you're going to spend a lot of time digging through endless configuration menus to set things up. Mostly the defaults are OK, but if you want to change something, you can. And that means more menus. And sometimes there are no defaults, like if you want a screen with additional time zones. So you have to go dive into the menus for those things.If you're OK dealing with complex little gadgets, the watch menus aren't a problem. But if twisty mazes of menu items put you off, this might not be the watch for you.The second and more serious flaw is the wrist-based heart rate monitor. Most of the time it's fine, but sometimes it gets confused and doubles your heart rate or adds 20-40 BPM. This tends to happen at the transitions between resting and aerobic activity, which is typically exactly when you'd start the timer and begin logging exercise data. And that's another trigger. Start an activity on the watch, and the heart rate data immediately spikes, even if you never get out of your chair.You can get it back on track by resetting the heart rate sensor, but that's kind of a pain in the ass. So that's something Garmin needs to fix before I could recommend this watch.

I hate writing reviews (especially bad ones) but figured I'd have to at least say something here, since I'm not going to return this watch. Just didn't want to let my disappointment go completely.I just want to say to anyone looking for accurate biometrics etc... keep shopping.For one, the heart rate monitor is grossly inaccurate as best. Even when I set the function to "Hike" when I'm on a hike (which seems to be recommended so that the HR monitor can gauge more accurately), the watch seems to be on a different hike altogether. Garmin apparently uses some sort of "new" technology to gauge your heart rate (like infrared light somehow sensing the volume of blood passing thru your skin or something) and they actually do mention on their help page that it may not be accurate, "depending on the activity." Well they're pretty right on there... it hasn't been at ALL for me. Unless I'm looking for my resting heartbeat while sitting at my desk or when I get up to make a sandwich, it's pretty much useless. for instance, I've taken the watch on multiple hikes in the mountains, wearing weight in my pack, sweating my a$# off... I look down and see I'm only at 82 bpm... wait, 83, ok...no...back to 82. I check my actual pulse and count my HR to somewhere around 150 - 160 bpm. I hike some more, stays the same, occasionally getting into the mid 90s. Sometimes, the watch will catch up and start counting semi-accurately around 1.5 miles into the hike etc but... not reliable at all. This seems like a pattern with this thing. I felt like the $200 ish price point was a steal for all this tech and I guess you get what you pay for. It seems to count steps ok (FYI my phone is also doing that) and compass seemed to work ok the couple times I popped into it but the Altimeter seems to be +/- 400 to 500 feet off on average, so I can't really use that function either. Overall I am disappointed in this thing and next time I'll likely go with a Suunto or something. I used to use Suuntos as a competitive skydiver years ago. They're altimeter was that good and accurate for an affordable price point (although you could set it to barometric pressure, so that's different than GPS... but still - c'mon Garmin, you're better than this!) The watch looks ok and is decently comfortable but kind of a TOY if you're looking for real world application. Also, the menu functions are clunky and I have had trouble navigating thru menus in any efficient way. I'd say this one is a good try, but a miss.

I have been using GPS trackers in my line of work for over 15 years and wanted to try this to see if it would work for me.After allowing the device to track for 24 hours I attempted to review the data the following day. VERY confusing software with a lot of glitches. It appears to be OpenMaps and the detail/quality is very poor. Nothing near Google Quality. After struggling with it for over two hours I was finally able to piece a chronological history together. Lots of reporting is missing from the map that is reported in the downloadable CVS.There are a few ways to review the stored data on their interface but no consistency with certain functions/features. Sometimes you can rest or click on a map pin and get the detailed time and GPS coordinates. Sometimes you can't. The times you can't, it is very troublesome.If you speed up the playback of a bread crumb trail in the history report, you can't slow it down afterward.If the device/vehicle stops, it will not begin tracking again until it's scheduled to, not when when it actually starts to move again. This can create a gap depending on how often you set your ping rate.I only see a benefit if you do real-time (1-minute pinging) tracking but there doesn't appear to be a bread crumb trail on the app map. Only the pins. Difficult to determine if the target is moving or stopped with only a pin in the map.  This is a little confusing when you start trying to follow activity as it unfolds. Other software I've used shows a pin for stopped and an directional arrow if moving. The battery may not last as long as it could in real-time mode.  I did purchase the extended battery and box and will later try to just let it run as a means to determine if my target is leaving the city or state when they are not supposed to.One other weird thing. You are only allowed up to 30 alerts to be sent to you via either email or text messaging. If your target starts and stops a lot, this can be a problem. Not sure what happens after 30 alerts is reached. I suspect you don't get anymore alerts. Or maybe you have to pay extra for them.Not a bad device overall for the price. If you buy one, don't go into it with great expectation. There are many more user friendly devices available for a little more cost. I 'm not sure if I'll buy a second one and just expect it to be disposable.

UPDATE: One less star because the SMS text based support has spammed my phone for days with nonsensical replies to problems I didn't report for Premium service which was canceled a week ago!  DO NOT USE THE SMS SUPPORT. Once they have your phone number, it is in their system to abuse.---------------------The Tiles work fairly well along with the app. The issues are that they do not live up to the marketing materials and support is sorely lacking.The stated ranges are very exaggerated in the real world and likely represent line of sight, no barrier testing. With walls and other interference, the ranges are 50% to 75% overstated. You can walk out of the room and the app will not find the Tile, yet the phone will still maintain Bluetooth connection with other things in the room!The crowd detection as described does not work well. In an area where the Android App indicated thousands of Tile users nearby, a Tile left out for detection in a busy area was never detected by other user’s devices and reported.  It did work when a test user was very close to the device (same room) and stationary, but again, not real world.The Android app is a bit odd, such as the traditional menu three vertical dots that most apps use for a menu but they do nothing in the app for each Tile where they are shown.  To see anything about the Tile, you have to tap its picture. If one searches for a device, that larger block never goes away and without a menu, there is no place to look to make it go away. Little things, yes, but software is about the little things.The available for an extra fee Tile Premium is worthless. The Smart Alerts function, which is mostly all you get, did not work at all. Only error messages saying on cannot do this with a shared Tile.  It is in Beta (so why would they make you pay to be their beta tester) so they might get it to work, but they never tell you when, just “soon.”That brings us to the worst part, support. Whilst trying to resolve the Smart Alert issues, it became apparent that the Premium Support offered via SMS test messages was subpar. Various random people would answer messages without any of the information from the previous messages. The suggestions were nearly random, all incorrect and went on for days, even when they were asked to stop on I had unsubscribed from the Premium Service. It was worthless and frustrating.Further, the traditional support via e-mail was slow, offered similar random and often incorrect and contradictory information, including that in regard to the phone number they’d now obtained via the SMS support.In none of the interactions with support did they ever offer a corrective action. I was told it would not work and that it should work! It was odd and appears that support is off shored if not somewhat just auto responses. It is like asking Alexa to tie your shoes.In the end, the Tiles themselves are functional and useful along with the Android Application. They can help you find your things but in a much more limited set of functional features than what is presented in their marketing materials. The process is adding Tiles and dealing with them worked great! The limits subset still leaves a very useful device, so they get three stars.  What ruins it is support, minus two stars, and if you buy there, know that you’ll likely be on you own.  There is no real support.

I ordered this because I was trying to get by without a smartphone and even if I did go back to one (to no one’s surprise, I did), I wanted to have something separate to navigate so I didn’t have to hear Siri cut in to the music to tell me about the upcoming turn. So all it did was have me go the opposite direction I needed to for a while. There was no traffic or road construction that necessitated me driving in the wrong direction, and the roads I was traveling on have been the same since my grandparents were kids, so it wasn’t an update issue either. While this was the only instance of it telling me to actually go the wrong directions, there were many times I would use it on routes that I knew and it would direct me to take a slower, more complicated route. It was only a difference of a few minutes, but why spend those few extra minutes driving unnecessarily?I also found the traffic feature to be entirely useless. I knew I was in traffic before it did.If you don’t have a smartphone and you want to avoid getting one, by all means do so and get this device for navigation. The pros:The display is brighter and sharper than older modelsA new feature is that when first calculating a new route the user can ask for it to calculate two routes and choose between them.  this feature would be better if it were activated by default, and it would be much better if the traffic information were more accurate (see below).The display can be seen clearly when wearing polarized sunglasses (Other screens, including older Garmins had a problem here)Accessories purchased for previous models also work with this one.Map and software updates can now be implemented over a Wifi connection to the internet.  Previous models required a cable connection through a computer.Vocal Instructions are clear.Visual directions are very clear.Voice recognition is improved from previous models, though still not great.  the weakness is forgivable because the unit runs all of the processing internally, whereas other voice recognition systems (e.g. Siri or Alexa) rely on internet connections.Touch screen is responsive.The cons:Though advertised as having traffic information independently of a phone, when not connected to the phone the traffic capability is much less accurate and less responsive than Garmin's previous models.  Traffic updates are late arriving, and are less likely to have details for surface streets (even major ones).  Travel time estimates, which had been very accurate with a previous model, are frequently off by 50%.If I had wanted to use my phone for navigation and traffic I could have done so without buying this unit.When connected via bluetooth to a phone, it occasionally and spontaneously takes over the audio, acting as a speakerphone.  That would be fine if I had instructed it to do this, but I didn't want it to.  I have three other bluetooth devices in my car already and they do not behave this way.  But the only way I have found to prevent it from doing this is to turn off the bluetooth connection to my phone.When acting as a speakerphone via bluetooth, I can hear fairly clearly but the person at the other end can not.

I'm gonna preface this with some personal info: I am a MMA fighter and BJJ competitor. I make my living as an athlete and instructor, so I exercise pretty much every day of my life. I average about 10-12 training sessions a week if you combine martial arts, cardio, and weight lifting. I'm not new to fitness, and as any professional athlete would, I take tracking my workouts and how my body responds to them seriously. I need accurate information extrapolated over time to build programs, keep my body on track and healthy, and to make sure i don't over or under train for competition. My performance and ultimately my livelihood are affected by that accuracy. Ive had this watch for several months, so now i feel comfortable in my familiarity to provide accurate feedback.The good: The watch is rugged. It can deal with getting banged up, sweated on, submerged, etc; just like you would expect it to be able to handle. It has a hefty amount of features... barometer, compass, altimeter, GPS (for various tasks such as tracking exercising distance, range finding, navigation, etc), weather, pulse oximeter, and so on.The bad: Unless you're sitting still the HR monitor is total dog sh#t, which is insane for a company that puts so much emphasis on their ability to track activity. I learned this day one and thought perhaps it needed a software update, to be restarted, to have the orientation on my wrist changed, to change the proximity on my wrist, to switch arms, etc etc etc. Nothing worked. I will be in the middle of a hard cardio session or doing sprints where my HR is between 150-180bpm, and it will tell me my BPM is 70. Wildly inaccurate. The only time it is accurate is when you are at complete rest, or when you use an external HR monitor connected to it. Even with an external HR monitor connected, as soon as it cycles itself back to the home screen (every 2 minutes it cycles back to home. I tried adjusting the settings to have it never cycle on its own, and it didn't change at all. Still cycles on its own. Definitely a software issue). I understand the most accurate HR readings come from multiple points of pulse reading, with most accurate being chest straps, but to not even register an elevation in HR at all is ridiculous at this price point. $30 HR monitors are more accurate. My FitBit Charge 4 was vastly more accurate on just my wrist, and at less than half the price. The solar option is a total waste of money unless you spend several hours a day in direct sunlight. I have even purposely left the watch in direct sunlight for 3 hours and the battery charge it gains is negligible. I live in Florida, literally "The Sunshine State" and its not worth the extra money. Maybe if you work in the sun all day or are stranded in the desert or on an island it would be worth it. For everyone else save the money and skip the solar upgrade. All of the basic functions are super convoluted through the watch interface, and equally so through the app. It takes 10 plus steps just to set or change an alarm. If done through the app its just as annoying, and requires a couple of syncs to make sure any changes to the previous settings take effect.For $400 Garmin dropped the ball hard AF on this one. This is my first Garmin watch, and probably my last because their first impression with me isn't a good one. I would rather spend half the money and have a smart watch that isn't as convoluted and inaccurate in its most basic functions.
Hard to use the button sequences to get basic navigation done.  Life is very complicated and I don't need another chore.

After a few months of research I settled on the Garmin Instinct because of the coupling of GPS functionality with a simple, rugged wristwatch design.However, after five days with it, I've decided to return it.  Here's why:1)  Images of the watch give the impression of a proportionately large screen.  However, in practice, I found that while running I couldn't check my data at a glance:  the actual screen area was just too small.  Meaning that I had to slow down and make an effort to hold my wrist steady to check my speed and distance.  Customizing the screen to show only one or two bits of data somewhat mitigates this, but, not satisfactorily.  And, then you have to switch between screens to see the different data.2)  Images of the watch, and many reviewer's comments, suggest a "Casio"/"G Shock"-like object.  I'd say that analogy only somewhat applies to its appearance, while the light weight of the watch, its soft, stretchy strap, and plastic used in the case don't quite impart Casio/G Shock quality.3)  While I have a soft spot for old school dot matrix/monochrome LCD displays, I find in practice that the slightly too low resolution of the Instinct's screen, and the design language of watch faces and widgets, do not speak to me.4)  Images of the watch suggest a "near-black" graphite color.  In reality, it is closer to grey.The above considered, I feel that I will be frustrated with this as an activity GPS watch, and won't appreciate it as a wristwatch between activities.While reviewers seem to concur that it is priced at a sweet spot in the sports watch/GPS/wearable market, I feel that evaluated on its own it's overpriced.However, some positives:1)  The screen and control customizability is excellent2)  The UI has a nice logic to it and in 20 minutes I was sufficiently familiar with it3)  The Garmin Connect iOS app is excellent4)  It seems to establish GPS/GLONASS/Galileo connectivity very quickly
